title: Sexual Selection
hook: Why does a peacock drag around a tail that makes it easy prey? Because for some traits, winning a mate matters more to evolution than simply surviving.
key_points: Sexual selection favors traits that help an individual win mates, not just survive.
It can produce extravagant features — like the peacock's tail — that survival alone would punish.
Mate choice (often by females) and competition between rivals are its two main forms.
Darwin proposed it to explain showy traits that ordinary natural selection couldn't.
content_html: Natural selection rewards survival, so how do you explain a peacock hauling around a tail that slows it down and advertises its location to predators? Charles Darwin's answer was sexual selection: evolution doesn't only favor traits that help you live longer, but also traits that help you reproduce. If a feature makes you more likely to win a mate, it can spread through a population even at a cost to your own survival.
extra_html: Sexual selection works through two channels. In mate choice, one sex — often females — prefers partners with particular traits, so those traits flourish across generations; peahens favoring the showiest tails is the classic example. In competition, members of one sex battle for access to the other, which favors weapons and size like a stag's antlers. Understanding Evolution from UC Berkeley notes that these pressures can drive runaway elaboration, producing the bright colors, songs, dances, and ornaments that fill the animal world. The result is a tug-of-war: survival pulls toward modesty while mating success pulls toward extravagance, and where the line settles shapes how a species looks and behaves.

related.title: Natural Selection
related.hook: No designer, no goal — just heritable variation, a struggle to survive, and the slow accumulation of whatever happens to work. That's how life adapts.

related.title: How New Species Form
related.hook: Split one population in two, let them drift apart long enough, and eventually they can no longer interbreed — that's speciation, the engine that fills the tree of life with branches.

related.title: Animal Adaptations
related.hook: A camel's hump, a chameleon's color, a polar bear's fat — these aren't accidents. Each is a trait shaped over generations to fit a particular way of life.

flashcards.back_html: Traits that help an individual win mates — through attracting partners or beating rivals — even when those traits make day-to-day survival harder.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the peacock's enormous tail a puzzle for ordinary natural selection?

choices.text: It's costly and dangerous, yet evolved anyway because it attracts mates
It helps the peacock fly faster from predators
It provides camouflage in the forest

flashcards.explanation_html: A huge tail is heavy and conspicuous, hurting survival. It persists because peahens prefer it, so the mating advantage outweighs the survival cost — that's sexual selection.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two main forms of sexual selection?

choices.text: Mate choice and competition between rivals

flashcards.explanation_html: One form is mate choice (one sex prefers certain traits in the other); the other is direct competition among members of one sex, such as males battling for access to females.
